claims.text: The stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by entropy of mixing.
Entropy of mixing stabilizes the disordered solid-solution phase at elevated temperatures.
The initial materials are multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles produced through physical and chemical fabrication approaches.
Temperature will be increased in a controlled manner across the stated service-temperature ranges.
Structural integrity and chemical composition will be monitored as temperature varies.
Elevated temperature increases the stabilizing effect of entropy of mixing.
Prevention of phase separation maintains nanoparticle structural integrity.
Nanoparticles exposed to higher temperatures will be more stable than nanoparticles maintained at room temperature.
High-temperature exposure will produce minimal structural degradation.
High-temperature exposure will produce minimal chemical change.
The proposed mechanism applies to multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles between 773 and 1923 K.
The exact relationship between entropy of mixing and stability under varying conditions is not fully established.
Significant structural degradation or phase separation at elevated temperature relative to the room-temperature control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction claims greater overall stability after high-temperature exposure than at room temperature, although the proposed entropy mechanism only addresses relative stabilization of a disordered phase and does not establish that heated nanoparticles should undergo less absolute degradation or chemical change than an unheated control.
